units.title: Unit 59 — Negative situations and feelings
learningObjectives: Describe anxiety, sorrow and anger through natural collocations without relying on literal translations.
Distinguish open expression from suppression of negative feelings and recognise the impact of criticism.
Use precise collocations for threats, conflict, irresponsible decisions and public reactions.

items.example: The sudden announcement came as a nasty shock to the whole department.
items.note: Nasty intensifies the unpleasant effect of an unexpected event; a shock is usually negative here.

items.example: In a fit of jealousy, he deleted every photo of his former partner.
items.note: A fit of jealousy is a sudden episode of intense emotion that may lead to impulsive behaviour.

items.example: She was sick with worry when her brother failed to return from the hike.
items.note: Sick with worry is an emphatic way to describe severe anxiety, usually without literal illness.

items.example: His parents were worried sick until the rescue team called.
items.note: Worried sick conveys the same extreme anxiety as sick with worry, but uses a different grammatical pattern.

items.pt: um plano maluco e pouco sensato
items.example: Their harebrained scheme to cross the desert without a guide quickly fell apart.
items.note: Harebrained describes an impractical or foolish plan, often with disapproval or humour.

items.example: One cruel review shattered the young musician’s confidence before the concert.
items.note: Shatter confidence means seriously undermine it; the verb stresses a dramatic loss.

items.pt: ficar ofendido ou se opor a algo
items.example: Several neighbours took exception to the suggestion that they had ignored the problem.
items.note: Take exception to is a relatively formal way to say that you strongly object or feel offended.

items.example: The prospect of repeating the difficult exam filled him with dread.
items.note: Fill someone with dread concerns fearful anticipation of a future event, not just a passing surprise.

items.example: She gave vent to her frustration by writing a long letter she never sent.
items.note: Give vent to is normally used for openly expressing negative feelings such as anger or frustration.

items.example: After several failed repairs, the mechanic admitted defeat and called a specialist.
items.note: Admit defeat means accept that an attempt will not succeed; it need not involve a competition.

items.example: If you bottle up your feelings for months, small problems can seem overwhelming.
items.note: Bottle up means suppress emotional expression, in contrast to giving vent to feelings.

items.example: Unclear deadlines can increase stress levels across the entire team.
items.note: Stress levels commonly combines with raise, increase or reduce; it describes perceived or measured strain.

items.pt: uma manifestação intensa e coletiva de pesar
items.example: The singer’s death prompted an outpouring of grief from fans around the world.
items.note: Outpouring of grief suggests a strong, widespread public expression of sorrow, especially after a death.

items.example: The passengers remained in a state of shock after the unexpected landing.
items.note: In a state of shock describes a sustained emotional reaction, not necessarily a medical diagnosis.

items.example: He struggled with inconsolable grief after losing his closest friend.
items.note: Inconsolable describes sorrow so intense that ordinary comfort does not relieve it.

items.example: The untreated infection may have hastened the patient’s death.
items.note: Hasten death means cause it to happen sooner; it does not necessarily identify the sole cause.

items.example: International observers warned of a threat of civil war following the disputed election.
items.note: Threat of civil war refers to the possibility of internal armed conflict, not to a declared war.

items.example: A threat of closure was hanging over the community centre for months.
items.note: A threat hanging over someone or something suggests an ongoing, unresolved danger.

items.example: She developed an intense dislike of crowded spaces after the incident.
items.note: Intense strongly modifies dislike; the noun commonly takes of before its object.

items.example: Approving the proposal without reading it was a serious lapse of judgement.
items.note: A lapse of judgement is a temporary failure to make a wise decision, rather than lasting incompetence.

items.example: The coach apologised for his disparaging remarks about the opposing team.
items.note: Disparaging remarks belittle someone or something; the combination is common in formal reporting.

items.example: Reports of further delays have fuelled fears that the bridge may be unsafe.
items.note: Fuel fears means increase existing anxiety or suspicion; it does not mean confirm the risk.

items.example: The workers said they had suffered rough treatment during the negotiations.
items.note: Suffer rough treatment describes being dealt with harshly; context determines whether it is physical or verbal.

items.pt: nas mãos de; por ação de
items.example: The village suffered serious losses at the hands of the invading forces.
items.note: At the hands of commonly identifies the agent responsible for suffering or harm.

items.example: With every road blocked, the drivers were left with little alternative but to turn back.
items.note: Typically followed by but to and an infinitive, this phrase stresses severely limited options.

items.example: The council took decisive action to prevent the damaged building from collapsing.
items.note: Take action is the natural verb–noun combination; decisive stresses prompt, effective intervention.

items.example: The protesters hurled insults at the minister as she left the building.
items.note: Hurl insults at someone is vivid and hostile; it describes forceful verbal attacks.

items.example: During the interview, the actor took a sideswipe at his former agent.
items.note: A sideswipe is an indirect critical remark, often inserted into a discussion of another topic.

items.example: It is a laughable idea that one small battery could power the whole factory.
items.note: Laughable conveys that an idea is absurd or unworthy of serious consideration, often dismissively.

items.example: The rising water level could pose a threat to homes near the river.
items.note: Pose a threat to means create a potential danger; pose naturally combines with threat or risk.

items.pt: estar prestes a ter uma surpresa desagradável
items.example: Anyone expecting an easy final exam may be in for a shock.
items.note: Be in for a shock warns of a likely unpleasant surprise in the near future.

items.example: The passengers were absolutely furious when their luggage went missing.
items.note: Absolutely is the natural intensifier with the extreme adjective furious; very furious is less idiomatic.

items.example: In a fit of temper, the child pushed his dinner plate aside.
items.note: A fit of temper means a sudden angry outburst; compare a fit of jealousy or anger.

items.pt: desfazer completamente as ilusões de alguém
items.example: The documentary shattered his illusions about the glamorous industry.
items.note: Shatter illusions means destroy comforting but mistaken beliefs; the object differs from confidence.

items.example: A stranger hurled abuse at the shop assistant over a minor mistake.
items.note: Hurl abuse at someone conveys aggressive verbal insults; unlike hurl an object, it is figurative.

items.example: A brief lapse of concentration caused her to miss the turning.
items.note: Lapse of concentration describes a temporary loss of attention; compare lapse of judgement.

items.example: Providing transport to remote villages poses a challenge for the region.
items.note: Pose a challenge refers to a difficulty to address, not necessarily a danger as in pose a threat.

items.example: The distant sirens filled the residents with foreboding.
items.note: Foreboding is an uneasy expectation of something bad, and commonly follows fill someone with.

units.title: Unit 60 — Positive situations and feelings
learningObjectives: Express achievement, relief, excitement and contentment through idiomatic combinations.
Discuss hopes, ambition, recognition and pleasure with accurate grammatical partnerships.
Distinguish degrees of optimism and fixed intensifiers used with positive feelings.

items.example: Completing the difficult course gave the apprentices a real sense of achievement.
items.note: Sense of achievement expresses satisfaction at succeeding through effort, not merely feeling happy.

items.example: Volunteering gave her a strong sense of purpose after retirement.
items.note: Sense of purpose is the feeling of having a meaningful aim; strong naturally intensifies it.

items.example: He heaved a sigh of relief when the missing dog finally came home.
items.note: Heave a sigh of relief expresses release from fear or tension after good news.

items.example: The opening notes of the symphony sent a shiver down my spine.
items.note: A shiver down the spine can reflect excitement or fear; context determines the emotion.

items.example: As the race began, she felt a surge of adrenalin.
items.note: Surge suggests a sudden increase in adrenaline-related excitement or nervous energy; adrenaline is another spelling.

items.example: After a short nap, I felt a burst of energy and tidied the kitchen.
items.note: Burst of energy describes a sudden, often short-lived increase in vitality.

items.example: The entire stadium was in a state of euphoria after the unexpected victory.
items.note: The conventional expression is state of euphoria, not place of euphoria.

items.example: Sitting by the quiet lake with a warm drink was sheer bliss.
items.note: Sheer bliss is an emphatic expression of complete pleasure or contentment, often calm rather than excited.

items.pt: o coração dispara de alegria ou emoção
items.example: My heart leapt when I saw my name on the list of successful applicants.
items.note: Heart leap is figurative for sudden strong feeling, often joyful surprise but sometimes alarm.

items.pt: uma ambição de toda a vida
items.example: Publishing a novel had been her lifelong ambition since childhood.
items.note: Lifelong ambition refers to a goal pursued or cherished for many years.

items.example: Opening his own bakery felt like a dream come true.
items.note: A dream come true names an achievement once hoped for, not necessarily a literal dream.

items.example: The organisers have high hopes for the new community programme.
items.note: Have high hopes for someone or something means expect a favourable outcome; the phrase can be disappointed.

items.example: The children jumped for joy when they heard about the extra holiday.
items.note: Jump for joy conveys exuberant happiness, whether or not someone literally jumps.

items.pt: estar muito a fim; muito entusiasmado
items.example: My cousin is dead keen to join the local theatre group.
items.note: Informal, especially British English; dead intensifies keen, and the phrase can be followed by to plus infinitive.

items.example: She found happiness in teaching music to young children.
items.note: Find happiness in identifies a source of lasting satisfaction; it does not imply discovering a physical thing.

items.example: The new restaurant did not live up to our expectations.
items.note: Live up to expectations means meet the standard people anticipated; the phrase often appears negatively.

items.example: Her experience with small teams may work to her advantage in the interview.
items.note: Work to someone’s advantage means produce a beneficial effect for them.

items.example: Finding the last available seat was pure luck.
items.note: Pure luck emphasises chance rather than effort or planning; not clean luck.

items.word: in the right place at the right time
items.pt: no lugar certo na hora certa
items.example: He met his future business partner by being in the right place at the right time.
items.note: The fixed expression attributes an opportunity partly to favourable timing and circumstances.

items.example: Doctors remain cautiously optimistic about her recovery.
items.note: Cautiously optimistic means hopeful while recognising real uncertainty and potential setbacks.

items.pt: ter grande satisfação ou prazer em
items.example: My father takes great delight in restoring old bicycles.
items.note: Take delight in is followed by a noun or -ing form and emphasises pleasure in an activity.

items.example: The students expressed profound admiration for the scientist’s persistence.
items.note: Profound strengthens admiration to indicate deeply felt respect.

items.example: After years of quiet work, the team finally got the recognition it deserved.
items.note: Recognition someone deserves means appropriate acknowledgement of their contribution or achievements.

items.example: She derives great pleasure from watching birds in the garden.
items.note: Derive pleasure from is somewhat formal and is followed by a noun or -ing form.

items.example: Several colleagues expressed admiration for his calm response to the crisis.
items.note: Express admiration for identifies openly voiced respect or appreciation; for introduces its object.

items.example: It was a great pleasure to meet the new volunteers.
items.note: A great pleasure is a conventional polite phrase; a big pleasure is not the usual collocation.

items.example: We had high hopes of finishing the restoration before winter.
items.note: High hopes of is followed by an -ing form and focuses on the hoped-for outcome.

items.example: Her wish to see the northern lights finally came true.
items.note: Dreams, hopes and wishes can come true; the subject is the hope itself, not the person.

items.example: Getting the only remaining ticket was a matter of pure luck.
items.note: A matter of pure luck attributes the outcome entirely or largely to chance.

items.pt: força de vontade pura e simples
items.example: Reaching the mountain summit in those conditions took sheer willpower.
items.note: Sheer willpower highlights intense determination, in contrast to achievements explained by pure luck.

items.example: A single encouraging teacher can have a profound effect on a student’s future.
items.note: Profound combines with effect as well as admiration, but the meaning shifts to deep influence.

items.example: It was sheer coincidence that both visitors arrived wearing the same jacket.
items.note: Sheer strengthens coincidence to stress complete chance rather than planning.
